facts.statement: 5 dispatchers built the next day's routes every morning in three shared spreadsheets.
Morning planning took about 2.5 hours, and trucks often left late because routes were not final.
Drivers received their stops on a printed sheet; changes during the day went by phone call.
Customers had no visibility, and the office took around 120 "where is my truck?" calls per day.
Late departures cascaded into missed delivery windows; the on-time rate was 81% in the last quarter before the project.
Trucks returned to the depot empty on 18% of route kilometres.
Proof of delivery was paper-based, and disputes took days to resolve.
Dispatchers spent the day on the phone with customers and drivers instead of planning.
Half of the billing disputes were about delivery signatures nobody could find.
A web dispatch console with a drag-and-drop route board and a live map of all trucks.
A driver app for Android and iOS with photo and signature proof of delivery and an offline mode that syncs when the signal returns.
A route optimiser that plans vehicle routes within customer time windows and driver hours, while dispatchers can still move stops by hand.
The optimiser suggests backhauls for return legs.
Customers receive ETA messages by SMS and email; the LLM-drafted text is checked against a fixed template before sending.
The driver app sends GPS pings every 30 seconds, and positions older than 5 minutes are shown as stale.
The rollout started with a pilot at one depot, where drivers gave feedback on the app daily.
The MVP went live at the first depot after 9 weeks, and all 3 depots were live after 14 weeks.
Morning planning is down to about 25 minutes for the whole fleet.
The on-time delivery rate reached 94%.
The empty-mile share fell to 11%.
61 of 64 drivers were using the app within two weeks of the all-depot rollout.
Customer status calls fell from 120 to 30 per day.
Customer status calls fell by 75% after launch.

facts.statement: The on-time rate went from 81 to 94 percent.
Customer calls are down to about 30 a day, mostly about changing delivery instructions.
Next.js and TypeScript for the web dispatch console.
Flutter for the Android and iOS driver app.
NestJS API on PostgreSQL with PostGIS for geospatial queries.
Python service using Google OR-Tools for vehicle routing with time windows.
Docker images on AWS ECS Fargate with RDS for PostgreSQL.
Bluefin runs 64 trucks from 3 depots and completes about 340 deliveries per day.
The existing in-cab telematics units had to stay, because their contract runs until 2027.
Rural routes have poor coverage, so the driver app had to work offline.
Go-live was required before the peak season in October.
Repository history: 29 commits between 2025-02-12 and 2025-05-20 by 4 contributors.
The telematics vendor's API documentation was incomplete, which cost the team a week.
The accounting export is still a manual step and is next on the list.
Every morning we rebuild the same puzzle from scratch in three spreadsheets, and by the time the trucks leave it's already wrong.
For the first time in years, my dispatchers go home on time and the phones are quiet.
Planning is done before the first coffee now.
